title: Articular and complementary infinitives

objectives.can: Read an infinitive completing a verb, and an infinitive with the article after a preposition, with its accusative subject.

explanation.summary: An infinitive is a verb turned into a kind of noun. Without the article it often completes another verb: δυνάμεθα γνῶναι, 'can we know'. With the neuter article, usually after a preposition, it becomes a small clause whose meaning depends on the preposition: μετὰ τὸ παραδοθῆναι τὸν Ἰωάννην, 'after John was arrested'. When the infinitive has its own subject, that subject is in the accusative.

sections.heading: The infinitive that completes a verb
body: Some verbs are incomplete without a second verb. In English: 'I can ...', 'I want ...', 'I am about ...', 'I begin ...'. In Greek the second verb is usually an infinitive. In Acts 17:19 the people ask Δυνάμεθα γνῶναι τίς … διδαχή; The finite verb Δυνάμεθα is first person plural; the infinitive γνῶναι tells what they can do. Other verbs of this kind: θέλω in John 1:43 (ἠθέλησεν ἐξελθεῖν, 'he wished to go out'), μέλλω in Acts 17:31 (μέλλει κρίνειν, 'he is about to judge'), ἄρχω in Luke 5:21 (ἤρξαντο διαλογίζεσθαι, 'they began to reason') and ζητέω in John 7:30 (ἐζήτουν … πιάσαι, 'they were seeking to seize').

The infinitive has no subject of its own here. Its subject is the subject of the finite verb. 'They began to reason' means that the same people began and reasoned. The tense of the infinitive tells about the kind of action, not about time. Aorist infinitives, as in ἀφεῖναι, name the action as a whole; present infinitives, as in ποιεῖν, see it as going on or repeated.

sections.heading: δεῖ and the accusative
body: The verb δεῖ, 'it is necessary', has no personal subject. It takes an infinitive for what is necessary, and often an accusative for the person who must do it. In Acts 16:30 the jailer asks τί με δεῖ ποιεῖν; Here με, 'me', is accusative, and ποιεῖν is the infinitive: 'what must I do?'. Grammarians describe με either as the object of δεῖ or as the subject of the infinitive. The second description is the one that carries over to the articular uses below.

This is the general rule: when an infinitive has a subject different from that of the main verb, the subject is put in the accusative. English says 'for him to do', or 'that he did'. Greek says the accusative and the infinitive.

sections.heading: The infinitive with the article
body: The article τό (or its genitive τοῦ or dative τῷ) can stand before an infinitive and turn the whole phrase into a noun. The article does not change the infinitive. It is neuter singular, and its case is the case the surrounding words need. In practice the construction is almost always governed by a preposition, and the preposition decides the sense. The table shows the common ones.

When the infinitive has a subject of its own, that subject is in the accusative and stands between the article and the infinitive or just after the infinitive. If the subject is the same as that of the main verb, it is usually not written at all. In John 2:24, διὰ τὸ αὐτὸν γινώσκειν πάντας, αὐτόν is the subject, and πάντας is the object: 'because he knew all'. The negative is μή, as in Luke 8:6, διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ἰκμάδα, 'because it had no moisture'.

head: Construction
Usual sense
Example
rows: εἰς τό or πρὸς τό + infinitive
εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι, 1 Thessalonians 3:2; πρὸς τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι, Matthew 26:12

sections.heading: Reading the senses with care
body: The senses in the table are what grammarians report as the usual uses. They are tendencies. The meaning of εἰς τό in particular varies. In 1 Thessalonians 3:2, εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς names the purpose of sending Timothy. In James 1:19, ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι is not 'quick in order to hear' but 'quick as regards hearing'. Read the sentence and choose the sense that fits.

The same goes for τοῦ with the infinitive. It is common for purpose, as in many places in Luke and Acts, but it can also give the content or result of something. In Acts 5:31, τοῦ δοῦναι μετάνοιαν follows the verb of exalting and says what the exalting was for or what it brings about.

sections.heading: A method for reading
body: When you meet an infinitive, ask three questions. Is there an article before it? If so, find the preposition and read the sense from it. Is there an accusative noun or pronoun beside it? If so, it is probably the subject of the infinitive. Is there a verb of wishing, being able, beginning, being about to or being necessary near by? If so, the infinitive probably completes it.

misunderstandings: Taking the accusative beside an infinitive as the object of the main verb. In πρὸ τοῦ ὑμᾶς αἰτῆσαι, ὑμᾶς is the subject of αἰτῆσαι: 'before you ask'.
Reading the article before an infinitive as 'the' in the English sense. It is a grammatical marker that makes a noun-like phrase, and usually it has no separate translation.
Reading the tense of the infinitive as time. In ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτούς the present infinitive does not make the event present for the writer; it shows the action as going on while another happens.
Giving every εἰς τό the sense of purpose. It is common, but James 1:19 shows another use.

deeper.heading: Why the infinitive can take a subject
body: The infinitive began, in the history of Greek, as a case form of a verbal noun. That is why it can be used with the article and why it can stand with a subject of its own. The accusative subject is the standard form in classical Greek and in the New Testament. The accusative subject is then a natural extension of that character.

deeper.heading: The infinitive and indirect speech
body: The accusative with the infinitive is also the usual form for reported speech in classical Greek: 'he said him to be a king'. The New Testament uses ὅτι more often, but the older form is still found. The pattern of an accusative subject and an infinitive is the same in both uses, so the skill of spotting the accusative subject carries over.

examples.analysis: Δυνάμεθα is the present middle of δύναμαι, first person plural, and γνῶναι is an aorist active infinitive. The infinitive completes the finite verb: 'can we know?' Its subject is the same as the subject of Δυνάμεθα, so no accusative is written. This is the plain complementary infinitive.

examples.analysis: δεῖ is the impersonal verb 'it is necessary'. με is accusative, naming the person who must act, and ποιεῖν is a present infinitive: 'what must I do?'. The question is the jailer's, and the accusative με is the subject of the infinitive in the sense used in this lesson.

examples.analysis: ἐν τῷ is the preposition ἐν with the article τῷ in the dative, governing the infinitive εἶναι. The accusative αὐτούς is the subject of εἶναι. The phrase gives the time: 'while they were there'. The main clause follows with ἐπλήσθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι.

examples.analysis: διὰ τό with an infinitive gives a cause. αὐτόν, accusative, is the subject of γινώσκειν, and πάντας, accusative, is its object. So the clause is 'because he knew all (people)'. The reflexive αὑτόν earlier in the verse is a different word, the object of ἐπίστευεν: 'he did not entrust himself to them'.

examples.analysis: πρὸς τό with an aorist infinitive gives a purpose: 'to prepare me for burial'. Here the infinitive has the same subject as the main verb, the woman, so no subject is written; the accusative με is the object of ἐνταφιάσαι, the person prepared. The main verb is ἐποίησεν, and the participle βαλοῦσα at the start is a circumstance.

practice.prompt: Δυνάμεθα γνῶναι τίς ἡ καινὴ αὕτη ἡ ὑπὸ σοῦ λαλουμένη διδαχή; What is the job of the infinitive γνῶναι (word 10)?

options: It completes Δυνάμεθα: 'can we know'
It is the main verb of the sentence and Δυνάμεθα is its subject
It names a person
It gives the time of the question
practice.explain: Δυνάμεθα, 'we are able', needs a second verb to say what we are able to do, and the infinitive supplies it. The subject of both is the same 'we'.

practice.prompt: καὶ ἤρξαντο διαλογίζεσθαι οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι. Who began, and who reasoned?

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Nobody: the infinitive is a noun meaning 'reasoning'
The scribes and Pharisees began, and Jesus reasoned
The scribes and Pharisees both began and reasoned: the infinitive shares the subject of ἤρξαντο
Jesus began, and the scribes and Pharisees reasoned
practice.explain: A complementary infinitive after a verb of beginning has the same subject as the finite verb. Both are plural, and the subject, οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι, is in the nominative.

practice.prompt: Καὶ μετὰ τὸ παραδοθῆναι τὸν Ἰωάννην ἦλθεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν. What does μετὰ τὸ παραδοθῆναι τὸν Ἰωάννην say, and who is the subject of the infinitive?

quoted.title: Mark
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: 'After Jesus went'; Ἰωάννην is the object of ἦλθεν
'After John was handed over'; τὸν Ἰωάννην, in the accusative, is the subject of the passive infinitive
'Before John was handed over'; Γαλιλαίαν is the subject
'In order that John be handed over'; Ἰησοῦς is the subject
practice.explain: μετά with the article and infinitive means 'after'. The infinitive παραδοθῆναι is passive, so the person handed over is its subject, put in the accusative: τὸν Ἰωάννην. ἦλθεν has its own subject, ὁ Ἰησοῦς.

practice.prompt: οἶδεν γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὧν χρείαν ἔχετε πρὸ τοῦ ὑμᾶς αἰτῆσαι αὐτόν. What is the subject of αἰτῆσαι (word 15)?

options: ὁ πατήρ: he asks
αὐτόν (word 16): 'before him asks'
ὑμᾶς (word 14): 'before you ask him'
There is no subject; it is a noun
practice.explain: The accusative ὑμᾶς is the subject of the infinitive, and αὐτόν, also accusative, is its object. πρὸ τοῦ gives the time: before you ask.

check.prompt: ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἐκεῖ ἐπλήσθησαν αἱ ἡμέραι. What does ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἐκεῖ say?

options: Purpose: 'in order that they be there'
Cause: 'because they were there'
A command: 'let them be there'
Time: 'while they were there'
check.explain: ἐν τῷ with an infinitive usually gives the time at which something happens. The accusative αὐτούς is the subject of εἶναι. The prepositional phrase does not give a purpose or a cause here.

check.prompt: αὐτὸς δὲ Ἰησοῦς οὐκ ἐπίστευεν αὑτὸν αὐτοῖς διὰ τὸ αὐτὸν γινώσκειν πάντας. In διὰ τὸ αὐτὸν γινώσκειν πάντας, who knows, and whom?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: Nobody knows: the infinitive is a noun
They know him: πάντας is the subject
All know all: both are subjects
He knows all: αὐτόν is the subject and πάντας the object
check.explain: Both αὐτόν and πάντας are accusative, so you read the sense. The pronoun αὐτόν stands before the infinitive and is the subject; πάντας follows and is the object. The phrase gives a cause.

check.prompt: βαλοῦσα γὰρ αὕτη τὸ μύρον τοῦτο ἐπὶ τοῦ σώματός μου πρὸς τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι με ἐποίησεν. What does πρὸς τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι με most likely express?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Condition: 'if she prepares me'
Time: 'while I was being prepared for burial'
Purpose: 'to prepare me for burial'
Concession: 'although she prepared me'
check.explain: πρὸς τό with an infinitive is a frequent way of giving purpose. The subject of the infinitive is the woman, as with ἐποίησεν, so none is written; με is the object, the person prepared. Time, concession and condition are not usual senses of this construction.

check.prompt: τῇ δόξῃ ᾗ εἶχον πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι παρὰ σοί. What is the subject of the infinitive εἶναι (word 16)?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: τὸν κόσμον (word 15), 'before the world was'
δόξῃ, 'before glory was'
There is none: the infinitive has no subject
The speaker, 'before I was'
check.explain: In this construction the subject of the infinitive stands in the accusative. The world is not the object of any verb here; πρὸ τοῦ with the infinitive means 'before the world was'.

check.prompt: ἐπέμψαμεν Τιμόθεον … εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς καὶ παρακαλέσαι ὑπὲρ τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν. What does εἰς τὸ στηρίξαι ὑμᾶς say about the sending?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Its purpose: 'in order to strengthen you'
Its opposite: 'so as not to strengthen you'
Its cause: 'because you strengthened'
Its time: 'after you were strengthened'
check.explain: εἰς τό with an infinitive often gives purpose. The subject of the infinitive is Timothy, who is also the object of ἐπέμψαμεν, so no subject is written; ὑμᾶς is the object of στηρίξαι. The two infinitives, στηρίξαι and παρακαλέσαι, share the one article.

check.prompt: ἔστω δὲ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι, βραδὺς εἰς τὸ λαλῆσαι. How is εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι (words 9–11) best read?

options: As respect: 'quick when it comes to hearing'
As purpose: 'quick, in order to hear'
As time: 'quick, while hearing'
As a command with no link to ταχύς
check.explain: εἰς τό is often purpose, but here it limits the adjective and says in what respect the person should be quick. The sentence shows why the senses in the table are tendencies, not rules.

check.prompt: Κύριοι, τί με δεῖ ποιεῖν ἵνα σωθῶ; Which description of με is correct?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It is the object of σωθῶ
It is a nominative subject of δεῖ
It is the accusative naming the person who must act; it goes with the infinitive ποιεῖν
It is a vocative, addressed to Κύριοι
check.explain: δεῖ is impersonal and takes an accusative of the person with an infinitive. με is accusative, not nominative. σωθῶ is passive and has its own subject, the same person.

check.prompt: ἡμέραν ἐν ᾗ μέλλει κρίνειν τὴν οἰκουμένην. How do μέλλει and κρίνειν (words 5–6) work together?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Both are in the future tense
μέλλει completes κρίνειν: 'he judges in order to be about'
μέλλει is the main verb and κρίνειν is a noun meaning 'judge'
μέλλει with the infinitive says he is about to judge, or will judge; τὴν οἰκουμένην is the object of κρίνειν
check.explain: μέλλω is one of the verbs that take a complementary infinitive. The infinitive κρίνειν carries the meaning, and its object τὴν οἰκουμένην is accusative. The subject of both is the same.

check.prompt: καὶ ἕτερον κατέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν καὶ φυὲν ἐξηράνθη διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ἰκμάδα. What does διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ἰκμάδα say?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Purpose: 'in order not to have moisture'
Concession: 'although it had moisture'
Time: 'while it had moisture'
Cause: 'because it had no moisture'; μή negates the infinitive
check.explain: διὰ τό gives a cause, and μή is the usual negative for the infinitive. The seed that fell on the rock withered for lack of moisture. The infinitive has no separate accusative subject, because its subject is the seed already named.

check.prompt: τοῦτον ὁ θεὸς ἀρχηγὸν καὶ σωτῆρα ὕψωσεν τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ δοῦναι μετάνοιαν τῷ Ἰσραήλ. How is τοῦ δοῦναι (words 10–11) best read?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: As 'of the giver': a noun in the genitive
As 'to give' repentance to Israel: purpose (or result), with the genitive article not translated
As a command: 'give repentance'
As a genitive absolute
check.explain: τοῦ with an infinitive is often purpose, though it can also express result or content, and the sentence is read for sense. There is no participle here, so no genitive absolute, and δοῦναι is an infinitive, not a noun.

reading.why: In Acts 16:27 the jailer ἤμελλεν ἀναιρεῖν ἑαυτόν (a complementary infinitive after μέλλω) and thinks ἐκπεφευγέναι τοὺς δεσμίους (an infinitive with an accusative subject). In 16:30 comes the question τί με δεῖ ποιεῖν. Three of this lesson's uses in five verses.
